title: Bloatware in Aftermarket Auto Parts
summary_raw:
This story is interesting:

One Civic owner purchased a cheap aftermarket head unit off Amazon, and decided to have Claude work its magic on it, like it would a smart TV. What was reportedly discovered isn’t surprising, but is worth knowing about.

Among the pre-installed bloatware—­or spyware, if you’re being less charitable­—was a voice assistant equipped with WebView, an Android system component that lets apps display content off the web. This apparently always used about a third of processing power, even while idle, which isn’t great. There were also Baidu location services, a call recorder (!), a DAB radio client that is pretty much useless in the U.S., and Adobe Acrobat, presumably so your passenger can entertain themselves with PDFs on the go...

title: Hiding Capabilities in AI Models
summary_raw:
Interesting research: “AI Models Can Provably Hide Arbitrary Capabilities”

Abstract: Capability evaluations aim to surface dangerous model behaviors before deployment, but their reliability depends on the assumption that hidden capabilities can be elicited. We show this assumption does not hold under adversarial conditions by constructing backdoor attacks that embed encrypted neural networks within host model weights, decrypting and executing them only upon receiving a secret trigger. Using digital lockers, these hidden circuits remain provably hard to elicit and interpret under cryptographic assumptions, even given full access to model weights, extending prior work from hiding fixed strings to arbitrary computations. We implement our proof of concept constructions in PyTorch and evaluate elicitation through fine-tuning, weight noising, gradient-based trigger search, and latent adversarial training, using a small chemical reaction prediction task as a proxy for CBRN-relevant capabilities. Our results demonstrate resistance to these methods and, together with our cryptographic guarantees, reveal a limit of elicitation-based capability audits. We release our models to support the improvement of defenses...

title: Compromised TLS Certificates
summary_raw:
The Indian CA eMudhra Limited has eight TLS certificates with laughably weak private keys:

The compromised eMudhra keys were defective at a level that’s challenging the imagination of many of the engineers studying the incident. A normal size for a NIST P-384 elliptic curve cryptography private key contains roughly 384 bits of entropy, a size allowing almost 2384, or a number with 116 digits, different possibilities. The private key sizes of the compromised keys ranged from 3 to 8 bits. Astonishingly, the private keys were 4, 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230, 237...

title: USN-8958-1: .NET vulnerabilities
summary_raw:
It was discovered that the .NET Blazor WebAssembly debug proxy did not
properly escape certain values. An attacker could possibly use this issue
to execute arbitrary code. The fix for this CVE was originally released via
USN-8942-1, but it was found to be incomplete. This issue only affected
dotnet10 and dotnet11. (CVE-2026-102870)

It was discovered that the Brotli decompression library used by .NET
incorrectly handled certain compressed streams. A remote attacker could
possibly use this issue to cause a denial of service or execute arbitrary
code. (CVE-2026-111497)

Alen Cheung discovered that .NET did not properly handle file ownership in
certain circumstances. An attacker could possibly use this issue to elevate
local privileges. (CVE-2026-114148)

title: USN-8955-1: nginx vulnerabilities
summary_raw:
It was discovered that nginx incorrectly handled certain configurations
using the alias directive together with rewrite rules. A remote attacker
could possibly use this issue to cause nginx to crash, resulting in a
denial of service, or execute arbitrary code.
(CVE-2026-15176)

It was discovered that nginx incorrectly handled map directives using
regex matching under certain circumstances. A remote attacker could
possibly use this issue to cause nginx to crash, resulting in a denial
of service, or execute arbitrary code.
(CVE-2026-93479)

It was discovered that nginx incorrectly handled HTTP/3 requests when
proxy_request_buffering was enabled. This issue only affected
Ubuntu 26.04 LTS and Ubuntu 26.10. A remote attacker could possibly use
this issue to inject data into proxied requests.
(CVE-2026-95101)

It was discovered that nginx incorrectly handled asynchronous file I/O
in certain configurations with Server Side Includes pages. A remote
attacker could possibly use this issue to cause nginx to crash,
resulting in a denial of service, or execute arbitrary code.
(CVE-2026-97205)

It was discovered that nginx incorrectly handled SSL session ticket keys
when configured with a shared session cache but without explicit ticket
key rotation. This issue only affected Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, Ubuntu 26.04 LTS,
and Ubuntu 26.10. A remote attacker
could possibly use this issue to forge client SSL sessions and bypass
client certificate verification.
(CVE-2026-97629)

title: [$] Removing binder.c
summary_raw: The final talk at Kangrejos 2026 was about the removal of the C implementation of Android's Binder driver, the primary interprocess communication mechanism used on Android devices. Carlos Llamas announced that he had deleted the C code to general applause, and then shared some insights about what went into replacing the C implementation. Alice Ryhl, who has worked on the Rust implementation for some years, added her own thoughts about what the most difficult and interesting parts of the transition were.

title: Haas: Postgres 19 is late, and it's AI's fault
summary_raw:
PostgreSQL developer Robert Haas writes about the struggles the project has encountered in putting together its next release.

In the end, I don't think that the delay in shipping PostgreSQL 19 is particularly concerning. It is not a long delay in the grand scheme of things, and it emerges directly from the project's concern for quality.

The long-term picture is less clear and in some ways more troubling: given that we have forty years of bugs that humans were unable to find but LLMs are quite capable of discovering, how are we ever going to catch up, and how will PostgreSQL continue to innovate? Right now, I'm not sure. What I do know is that I, and many others, are working really hard to figure it out.

LWN looked at the PostgreSQL 19 release and its challenges in September.

title: Remote code execution on Linux systems with multipath TCP
summary_raw: On October 27, LLM provider Anthropic reported on a remotely exploitable use-after-free bug affecting systems with multipath TCP listeners open. The bug works by triggering a response to a retransmitted SYN packet at the same moment that the TCP connection is established in another thread, causing the first thread to access the connection's options structure after the second thread has freed it. The first thread can then disclose kernel memory or cause a buffer overflow, writing an attacker-controlled payload. The fix was to only free the structure after an RCU grace period. On October 29, the Go security team advised that all programs written in Go use multipath TCP by default, so many systems may be unknowingly vulnerable. And, of course, there is always the possibility of related bugs in other sections of the TCP stack. Users may be wise to update to a patched kernel as soon as one becomes available for their distribution.

title: [$] Containers as a recognized kernel object
summary_raw: The foundation of the design for containers in the kernel is that there isn't one; there is no container abstraction that the kernel recognizes. Instead, the kernel provides a long list of components — namespaces, control groups, sandboxing mechanisms, and more — along with a note that says, in effect, "some assembly required". There have been attempts (repeatedly) over the years to turn containers into first-class objects with kernel support, but they have never gotten far. Now Josef Bacik is making a try with a concept that he calls "cells".

title: A report from the LPC sched_ext microconference
summary_raw:
The Linux Plumbers Conference blog has a report from the sched_ext microconference held in Prague.

Three main topics dominated the discussions
  • Priority inversion and how to handle it in sched_ext: lock holder and lock waiter preemption, time slice extension, and making proxy execution work together with BPF schedulers.
  • Paravirtualized scheduling: letting the host and guest schedulers cooperate across the VM boundary, with sched_ext as the policy engine on the host.
  • Device and topology-aware scheduling: using hardware feedback (Intel HFI), device/accelerator locality and cache topology to drive task placement.

title: [$] The campaign to push Northstar into Linux distributions
summary_raw: There is not a broad selection of mature, open-source web-browser engines for Linux users. Most of the browsers available for Linux are based on one of just three projects: Chromium's Blink, Firefox's Gecko, or WebKit. A new entrant would generally be seen as a welcome alternative, but the recent campaign to push one of the LLM-written Nordstjernen browsers into Debian and Arch Linux has raised some questions about the project's development and security processes.

title: Redox OS ring buffers project summary
summary_raw:
The Redox OS project, which is a Unix-like microkernel-based operating system written in Rust, has published a report on the work that it has done in the last year to implement io_uring-like I/O.

Last year, the Redox team received a grant to develop io_uring-like Ring Buffer support at the system task level, as a first step towards ring buffer communications between the application and the majority of system services. This phase of the work finished up in September, as the last pieces were put in place.

[...] In addition to implementing the Ring Buffer machinery for our system services and drivers that can support it, an io_uring and liburing-like API for applications was completed and demonstrated. There was also substantial work done on support crates, including an async executor for drivers.

And there was some very exciting work on various performance improvements, to allow much faster switching between applications and their system services. But I will let the team tell you all the technical details.

title: Robinson: Raspberry Pi 5 on Fedora
summary_raw:
Peter Robinson has written a blog post about the current state of Fedora support for Raspberry Pi 5 devices. According to Robinson, the upcoming Fedora 45 release will work—with caveats—on all variants of the Raspberry Pi Model 5B; the Compute Module 5 and Pi 500+ are still works in progress.

For Fedora 44 release you need to have a temporary workaround when booting. If you update to the latest kernel/firmware straight away this isn't then needed beyond the first boot. The workaround isn't needed for Fedora 45 so if you're going to try this out I suggest you go and grab your favourite flavour of Fedora from the Fedora 45 release candidates and jump straight in there! You will get an accelerated desktop with storage/network/USB. There's not currently any support for sound and a number of other things.

See Robinson's post for instructions on creating an Fedora image to use with a Raspberry Pi 5.

title: [$] Guidelines for panics in kernel code
summary_raw: Alexandre Courbot spends most of his time working on the kernel doing code reviews. Recently, he's been wondering about what the standards should be for when Rust code is allowed to panic, and how it should do error handling more generally. Unlike many of the other talks at Kangrejos 2026, his talk was not presenting some existing work, but rather hoping to solicit opinions on the topic from the assembled Rust for Linux developers. He brought along a collection of tricky cases that he had run into recently to prompt discussion.
